hints: Start by picturing the levels of structure - three polypeptides wound into a triple helix, then many helices packed together into a fibre. What type of bond could link separate molecules together?
Think about strength in terms of bond strength and weak spots. If molecules were laid end-to-end exactly in line, where would the fibre be most likely to break?
Now think about skin - it gets pulled and stretched in many different directions, not just one way. How would the arrangement of whole fibres in the tissue help with this?
walkthrough:
Linking molecules with strong bonds**
Think of a collagen fibre as a thick rope made of many triple-helix molecules. These molecules are not just tangled together, they are chemically tied to each other by covalent bonds between their R groups or side chains. Covalent bonds are very strong and need a lot of force to break, so this cross-linking stops the molecules sliding past each other when pulled.

Staggering removes weak points**
The molecules do not line up end-to-end. They are staggered and overlapping, like bricks in a wall. This means the ends of molecules never line up in one place to create a weak line where the fibre could snap. Force is spread evenly along the whole fibre.

Strength in all directions for skin**
Skin needs to resist pulling from all directions. In skin the collagen fibres are not all parallel. They are laid down in layers with fibres running in different directions. This arrangement gives high tensile strength in many directions, so the skin resists tearing however it is stretched.

Final answer: Covalent bonds form between R groups of adjacent collagen molecules. Covalent bonds are strong. Molecules are staggered / overlapping so there are no weak areas. In skin, fibres are arranged in layers running in different directions, giving tensile strength in different directions.

hints: Look carefully at Fig. 6.1. Find the optimum pH at the peak of the curve and read off the activity at pH 8.0. What does the drop from 100% to about 40% tell you about how well the enzyme is working?
Remember that pH affects charges on R groups. Which relatively weak bonds that hold the 3D shape of the enzyme together would be broken or altered by extra OH- ions at higher pH?
walkthrough:
Reading the graph and linking pH to shape**
From Fig. 6.1 the optimum pH is about pH 7.3 to 7.5 where activity is 100%. At pH 8.0 activity has fallen to about 40%. A change in pH changes the $H^+$ and $OH^-$ concentration, which changes the charges on the R groups of amino acids. This breaks or alters the ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme in its precise 3D shape.

From altered active site to lower activity**
When those bonds are disturbed, the shape of the active site changes. It is no longer fully complementary to the substrate collagen. Fewer collagen molecules can fit correctly into the active site, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time and the rate of breakdown falls. This is partial denaturation, not full destruction of the enzyme.

Final answer: At pH 8.0, ionic and hydrogen bonds between R groups are broken / altered, so the shape of the active site is altered. The active site is no longer / less complementary to collagen so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form, lowering activity.
